why_this_tool: Redis exposes every caching decision in this lesson as something you can set and observe on a laptop: per-key TTLs, a memory limit, selectable eviction policies and hit and miss counters.
alternatives: Memcached is a simpler multi-threaded key-value cache with no rich data types or persistence; Valkey is the open source fork that keeps the same commands and protocol; Caffeine is an in-process local cache for the JVM with no network hop; ElastiCache is a managed cloud service that runs Redis-compatible engines for you; Varnish caches whole HTTP responses in front of a service; a CDN caches responses at the edge, close to users.

setup.do: Install Docker and start a single Redis Open Source container on the default port.
setup.done_when: The container shows as running and the server answers PONG to a PING.
setup.why: A container gives you a disposable cache server that you can stop, wipe and restart, which the later cold start and outage steps rely on.

setup.do: Install the redis-py client library into a fresh Python virtual environment.
setup.done_when: Importing the redis module in a Python session raises no error.
setup.why: The read and write patterns live in application code, so you need a client to write them rather than only typing commands by hand.

setup.do: Install Redis Insight and connect it to the local server.
setup.done_when: Redis Insight lists your local database and shows an empty key list.
setup.why: A visual key browser lets you watch keys appear, expire and get evicted while your scripts run.

setup.do: Check the Redis Data Integration quickstart prerequisites against your laptop so the last step is ready to run.
setup.done_when: You have a written note of which prerequisites you already meet and which you must install before the last step.
setup.why: The final production-like step keeps a cache in sync with a source database and needs a local VM or local cluster plus PostgreSQL, which is worth confirming early.

steps.do: Run your first SET and GET against the local server with the Redis command line interface.
steps.done_when: A value you stored under a key comes back unchanged from a GET.
steps.why: A cache is first of all a fast key lookup, and typing the commands by hand shows the request and reply model before any library hides it.

steps.do: Create a key naming scheme for cached objects, with an entity name, an identifier and a version segment, and store a few entries under it.
steps.done_when: Redis Insight shows your sample keys grouped under the prefixes you designed.
steps.why: Key design decides what you can invalidate together and how you roll out a changed value format without reading stale shapes.

steps.do: Read the LangCache architecture section to see a cache modelled as lookup, miss, fill and store; it is a hosted cloud service, so the local substitute is the exact-match string cache you build in the next step.
steps.done_when: You can sketch the hit path and the miss path from memory and name where the entry is written.
steps.why: The same hit, miss and fill flow underlies every cache, and seeing it for semantic matching makes clear which parts are general and which are specific to one use.

steps.do: Write a cache-aside read function with redis-py that checks Redis first, falls back to a slow stand-in data source on a miss and then stores the result.
steps.done_when: The first call for an identifier takes the slow path and the second call returns quickly from Redis.
steps.why: Cache-aside is the most common read pattern, and writing it yourself exposes the miss path that write-through and write-behind move elsewhere.

steps.do: Configure a TTL on every entry your function writes, and delete the key whenever the stand-in source is updated.
steps.done_when: The remaining time to live on a key counts down, the key disappears at zero, and an update to the source removes it at once.
steps.why: Expiry bounds how stale a value can get without any coordination, while explicit deletion on write is the invalidation path for data that must be fresh sooner.

steps.do: Write a short-lived lock key with an expiry so that only one caller rebuilds a missed entry, then run twenty concurrent readers against an expired hot key.
steps.done_when: Your stand-in source logs a single rebuild for the twenty concurrent readers instead of twenty.
steps.why: When a popular key expires, every reader misses at once and stampedes the source; a lock that expires on its own lets one caller refill without risking a stuck lock.

steps.do: Configure a small maxmemory limit on the server and load more cached entries than fit.
steps.done_when: The reported memory use stays at or under the limit while you keep writing.
steps.why: Sizing a cache means deciding how much of the working set to hold, and a deliberately small limit lets you watch what happens at the boundary.

steps.do: Compare the noeviction, allkeys-lru, allkeys-lfu and volatile-ttl policies by replaying the same skewed read and write workload under each.
steps.done_when: You have a small table of hit rate and write errors per policy for the same workload.
steps.why: The policy decides which data survives memory pressure and whether writes fail instead, so the right choice depends on your access pattern and on whether every key has a TTL.

steps.do: Run a cold start by emptying the cache and replaying the workload while reading the hit, miss and evicted key counters from INFO.
steps.done_when: You can plot the miss count rising steeply after the wipe and flattening as the cache warms.
steps.why: An empty cache sends the full read load to the source, and the counters show how long the warm-up lasts and how much load the source must absorb during it.

steps.do: Reproduce the whole experiment from a pinned Redis image tag, then stop the container mid-run and add a timeout and fallback so reads still succeed from the source.
steps.done_when: A fresh machine reproduces your numbers from the pinned image, and reads keep returning correct values while the container is stopped.
steps.why: A pinned image makes your results repeatable on any machine or in CI, and stopping the server proves whether the cache is an optimisation or a hidden dependency.

steps.do: Compare an in-process dictionary cache placed in front of Redis with Redis-only reads, then read how eviction behaves across replicated databases to reason about distributed and edge copies.
steps.done_when: You have latency figures for both layouts and a one-paragraph note on which copy can be stale and for how long.
steps.why: A local cache removes the network hop but each process holds its own possibly stale copy, while a shared or replicated cache trades latency for consistency across instances.

steps.do: Deploy the Redis Data Integration quickstart pipeline on a local VM or local cluster so changes in PostgreSQL flow into Redis, then change a source row.
steps.done_when: A row you update in PostgreSQL shows its new value in the matching Redis key without your application writing it.
steps.why: Feeding the cache from the database change stream is a production-grade alternative to cache-aside: the cache is kept warm and current without application invalidation code.
